78.title: Shiphrah and Puah (Exodus 1:15–21)
78.hook: two midwives quietly refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the baby boys
78.howItsDone: Jewish teaching often holds up Shiphrah and Puah as models of moral courage, and the Talmud credits righteous women with the redemption from Egypt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: a new Pharaoh, a growing people, and fear turned into slavery. Your line was fear forgets. Today, fear goes one step further, and two women stand in its way.

The labor isn't working; the Israelites keep growing. So Pharaoh does something worse. He calls in two women, midwives, the ones who help the Hebrew mothers give birth. And the text, which leaves out so many names, gives us theirs: Shiphrah and Puah. Pharaoh's order is simple and monstrous. When you deliver a Hebrew woman's baby, look. If it's a boy, kill it. If it's a girl, let her live. Two midwives, alone, facing the king of Egypt.
screen: `THE LABOR ISN'T WORKING.` → `TWO MIDWIVES, CALLED TO PHARAOH.` → `IF IT'S A BOY, KILL IT.`

segments.voice: They don't argue. They don't lead a protest. They just don't do it. "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." Feared God: the Hebrew means something like reverence, a sense that there's something above the king. Pharaoh calls them back. Why have you let the boys live? Their answer is brilliant. The Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women. They're lively, full of life; they give birth before the midwife even gets there. Pharaoh can't check. They walk out alive, and the text says God dealt well with the midwives, and made them houses: families, households of their own. Now, a puzzle. The Hebrew can be read two ways: Hebrew midwives, or midwives to the Hebrews. If they're Hebrew women, they're protecting their own people. Some medieval commentators, like Abarbanel, suggested they were Egyptian women protecting someone else's babies. One opinion in the Talmud says they were Moses' own mother and sister, under other names. The text doesn't settle it. What it does make plain: the first people in the book of Exodus to stand up to Pharaoh aren't prophets or soldiers. They're two working women with a job to do, who wouldn't do it wrong. Some modern writers call it civil disobedience. Quiet, practical, and brave.

It doesn't have to be dramatic. Picture yourself just not doing it, quietly, the way the midwives did.
Shiphrah, one of the two midwives Pharaoh ordered to kill the baby boys, who quietly refused. The Talmud links her name to making beautiful.

79.title: A basket on the Nile (Exodus 2:1–10)
79.hook: Yocheved hides her baby, Miriam watches, Pharaoh's daughter draws him out
79.howItsDone: Jewish tradition honors the women of the Exodus story, Yocheved, Miriam, the midwives and Pharaoh's daughter, whom the rabbis call Bityah, and teaches that Israel was redeemed from Egypt in the merit of righteous women.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiphrah: two midwives quietly refused to kill the baby boys. Your line was the midwives said no. Pharaoh's next order goes to everyone: throw every Hebrew boy into the river.

If you've ever had a newborn in the house, you know: they're not quiet. They cry at three in the morning. They cry when you're trying to be invisible. Now imagine hiding one, in a country where soldiers are looking for baby boys. A woman from the tribe of Levi gives birth to a son. She sees that he's good, the text says, and she hides him for three months. Then she can't anymore. So she makes a decision no parent should ever have to make.
screen: `A NEWBORN IS NEVER QUIET.` → `HIDDEN FOR THREE MONTHS.` → `THEN SHE CAN'T ANYMORE.`

segments.voice: She takes an ark of bulrushes, waterproofs it with pitch, puts the baby inside, and sets it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile. The Hebrew word for this little basket is tevah, the same word used for Noah's ark, and nowhere else in the Torah. Once, a box on the water saved all of life. Now a box on the water carries one baby. Then a small, enormous detail: "And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him." She isn't named here, but later we learn: Miriam. A young girl, hiding in the reeds, watching. Pharaoh's own daughter comes down to bathe. She sees the basket, opens it, and the baby is crying. She has compassion on him. She knows exactly what this is: one of the Hebrews' children. The daughter of the man who ordered the boys drowned decides to save one. Now Miriam moves. She steps out of the reeds: shall I go and find you a Hebrew woman to nurse the baby for you? Go, says the princess. Miriam runs and brings the baby's own mother, Yocheved, as the text later names her, and now she's being paid to nurse her own son. When he's older, she brings him back to the palace, and Pharaoh's daughter names him Moshe, Moses: "Because I drew him out of the water." Three women. A mother who let go, a sister who watched, and a princess who broke her father's law. The rabbis give that princess a name: Bityah, daughter of God.

80.title: Moses goes out and sees (Exodus 2:11–15)
80.hook: the prince goes out to his people and sees their burdens
80.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point to this passage as the first sign of Moses' leadership: before God speaks to him, he goes out to his people and sees their suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tevah, the basket on the Nile: a mother let go, a sister watched, a princess drew him out. Your line was someone watches the basket. Now the baby is a grown man, raised in a palace.

Some people grow up very close to suffering, and never see it. The people who clean their houses, cook their food, build their buildings, are right there, and somehow invisible. Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, with food, clothes, and a princess for a mother. Just outside, his own people were making bricks under the whip. He could have lived his whole life without looking. The Torah skips his entire childhood in a single verse. Then it says: when Moses had grown up, he went out.
screen: `RIGHT THERE, AND INVISIBLE.` → `A PRINCE IN PHARAOH'S PALACE.` → `ONE DAY, HE WENT OUT.`

segments.voice: Every word counts: "he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." His brethren: he knows who they are. He's not a tourist. The midrash takes that word looked seriously. Moses didn't just glance, it says. He saw their loads and wept, and put his own shoulder under the bricks to help, one person at a time. Then he sees something worse: an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. The text slows down: he looked this way and that way, and saw there was no man. And he struck the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand. The Torah doesn't praise it, and doesn't condemn it. The rabbis read that look in different ways. Some say he looked to be sure no one would see. Others say he looked to see whether anyone else would step in, and there was no one; so he did. The next day he goes out again and sees two Hebrews fighting each other. He tries to stop them, and one turns on him: "Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?" Are you going to kill me too? The secret is out. Pharaoh hears and wants him dead, and Moses runs, all the way to Midian. There, sitting by a well, he sees shepherds pushing some young women away from the water, and he stands up and helps them. He can't stop seeing. That's the first thing the Torah tells about the man who will lead the Exodus, before any miracles. He went out, and he saw.

segments.voice: Think of a burden someone near you carries that's easy not to see: someone you pass every day on the way to work, a neighbor who's struggling, people in your own city living a very different life than yours. Don't solve it, and don't look away either. Just see it, honestly, for a minute.

81.title: The burning bush (Exodus 3:1–6)
81.hook: a bush burns and is not consumed, and Moses turns aside to look
81.tomorrow: a name that is a verb
81.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads the burning bush as the moment Moses is called, and teachers often use it to talk about noticing holiness in ordinary places; the Hebrew word for bush, sneh, is heard as an echo of Sinai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayar: a prince who looked at his people's burdens, and ran for his life. Your line was he went out and saw. Now he's a shepherd in Midian, many years later.

Moses has a quiet life now. He married Tzipporah, one of the young women he helped at the well. He has a son. He keeps sheep for his father-in-law, Jethro. Years go by; the palace is a memory. One day he leads the flock deep into the wilderness, to a mountain called Horeb. Ordinary work, an ordinary day. Out of the corner of his eye, he sees a bush on fire. In the desert, dry brush catches. Plenty of people would keep walking.
screen: `A SHEPHERD NOW, YEARS LATER.` → `AN ORDINARY DAY AT HOREB.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's what makes it strange: "the bush was not consumed." It's burning, and it doesn't burn up. Moses says: "I will turn aside now, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." Then the verse that makes the whole story: "And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush." Read it slowly. The call comes after Moses stops. It's as if the fire was burning for anyone who'd notice, and Moses was the one who did. Some teachers have pointed out that you'd only know the bush wasn't burning up if you watched it for a while. A glance wouldn't tell you. You'd have to stay. Then God calls: "Moses, Moses." And he answers: "Here am I." Hineni, the same word Abraham said. Then: don't come closer; "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Ordinary dirt, on a mountain where sheep had been grazing, and the text calls it holy ground. Why a thorn bush, a lowly desert plant? The midrash answers: to show that God is with the people in their suffering, in the thorns, not only in the cedars. Some have read the bush that isn't destroyed as a picture of Israel itself, burning under slavery, and still there. Moses hides his face, afraid to look at God. He's about to find out why he was called.
screen: `THE BUSH WAS NOT CONSUMED.` · `I WILL TURN ASIDE NOW, AND SEE.` · `WHEN GOD SAW THAT HE TURNED ASIDE.` · `THIS IS HOLY GROUND.` · then, large: `HERE AM I.`

segments.voice: Find one ordinary thing right where you are: light on a wall, the grain of a table, your own hand, a plant, a sound outside. Turn aside to it the way Moses did, and stay with it longer than you normally would, as you'd watch a fire that doesn't go out. What do you see now that you didn't see a minute ago?
Hineni, here am I, the word Moses answers with at the bush, the same word Abraham once said when God called him.

82.title: A name that is a verb (Exodus 3:13–15)
82.hook: Moses asks God's name and hears "I AM THAT I AM"
82.carry: I will be what I will be
82.howItsDone: Jews do not pronounce the four-letter name of God; in prayer and Torah reading they say Adonai, and in everyday speech many say HaShem, the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hineni: Moses answered the call at the bush, the same word Abraham once said. Your line was turn aside and see. Today, Moses asks a question back.

From the bush, God tells Moses: I have seen the affliction of my people, I have heard their cry, and I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring them out. And Moses, standing barefoot on holy ground, asks a very practical question. When I tell the Israelites the God of your fathers sent me, they're going to ask: what's his name? What do I tell them? Who are you, exactly? The answer is not quite a name.
screen: `I HAVE SEEN, I HAVE HEARD.` → `THEY WILL ASK, WHAT IS HIS NAME?` → `WHAT DO I TELL THEM?`

segments.voice: God answers: "I AM THAT I AM." And then: tell them, "I AM hath sent me unto you." In Hebrew: Ehyeh asher ehyeh. Here's what an English Bible can hide. Ehyeh is a verb, from the Hebrew root for to be, in a form that usually points forward, into the future, or into something still going on. So it can mean I am who I am. Or I will be what I will be. Or I will be there, as I will be there. The old Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917 prints I AM THAT I AM, and notes in the margin that it could also be read I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE. Moses asked for a name, a label you can hold. What he got was more like a promise, and a mystery. The Talmud hears the promise: God meant, I will be with them in this trouble, and in troubles still to come. Rashi passes that on. Other thinkers, like Maimonides, heard something about God's very being, existence itself, beyond any name. Both readings stay in the tradition. Then God gives one more name, made of four Hebrew letters, which tradition links to the same root: the name Jews treat as too holy to pronounce. In prayer they say Adonai, my Lord, and in ordinary talk, HaShem, which just means the Name. This is my name forever, God says. Read the way the Talmud reads it, it doesn't say what God is. It promises God will be there, and leaves the how open.

segments.voice: Think of something you can't pin down: a question about God, about your future, about someone you love. Notice the urge to label it and settle it, then let it stay open; you don't have to know how it turns out. If you pray, you can hold the words I will be what I will be; if not, let the question breathe with you.
Ehyeh. I will be, or I am. The name God gives Moses from the bush: a verb, a presence, and a promise.
Your line: I will be what I will be. Some names are promises. See you tomorrow.

83.title: Who am I? (Exodus 3:11, 4:10–17)
83.hook: Moses protests that he is slow of speech; Aaron will speak for him
83.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls Moses the greatest of the prophets and also the humblest of men, and teachers often point to his reluctance at the bush as part of why he was chosen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ehyeh: a name that is a verb. Your line was I will be what I will be. Today, that same word comes back as a promise to a man who doesn't want the job.
screen: `I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.`

segments.voice: Someone gets offered something big: a promotion, a speech at a wedding, a role they never imagined. And before they even think, the words come out: me? Oh, no. I'm not the right person. Moses is standing at a burning bush, being told by God himself to go and free a nation of slaves. And he spends most of the conversation trying to get out of it.
screen: `ME? I'M NOT THE RIGHT PERSON.` → `A BURNING BUSH, A HUGE JOB.` → `MOSES TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.`

segments.voice: His first objection is the biggest: "Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?" A shepherd. A fugitive. A man who ran away. God doesn't argue with him about who he is. God says: "Certainly I will be with thee." In Hebrew, ki ehyeh imach. There's yesterday's word: ehyeh, I will be. The answer to who am I is: it's not only about you. Moses keeps going. What if they ask your name? What if they don't believe me? Each time, God answers. Then Moses gets personal: "I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." I'm not a speaker. Never have been. Nobody knows exactly what he means. A stammer? Rusty Hebrew after years in a palace, or rusty Egyptian after years in the desert? A midrash tells that as a baby in Pharaoh's house, he burned his tongue on a coal. The Torah doesn't explain. God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?" I'll be with your mouth. Finally Moses just says it: please, send someone else. And God is angry; the text says so. But God doesn't take the job away, and doesn't pretend the weakness isn't real. Your brother Aaron is coming to meet you, God says, and he speaks well. He'll be your mouth, and you'll tell him what to say. So the man the Torah later calls a prophet like no other didn't think he could speak, and needed his brother's help to do it. The weakness stayed. He was sent anyway, and not alone.

84.title: Let my people go (Exodus 5)
84.hook: the first demand, and Pharaoh makes the bricks harder to make
84.howItsDone: At the Passover seder Jews retell the slavery in Egypt as their own story, and the words let my people go have been taken up by many freedom movements, including the African American spiritual Go Down, Moses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ehyeh: I will be with you, God's answer to a man slow of speech. Your line was slow of speech, still sent. This week ran from two brave midwives to a basket, a prince who saw, a bush, a name, and a reluctant prophet. Today he finally walks into the palace.

You know these four words even if you've never opened the book of Exodus. Enslaved people in America sang them in the fields: go down, Moses, tell old Pharaoh, let my people go. People marching for freedom have painted them on signs. But the first time they were said, in the Torah, two brothers carried them into a throne room: Moses and Aaron, standing before the king of Egypt. Aaron speaking, Moses beside him.
screen: `GO DOWN, MOSES.` → `TWO BROTHERS IN A THRONE ROOM.` → `THE FIRST TIME IT'S SAID.`

segments.voice: They say: thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Let My people go, that they may hold a feast unto Me in the wilderness." Pharaoh answers with a sneer: "Who is the LORD, that I should hearken unto His voice?" I don't know him, and I won't let Israel go. Then he does what every tyrant knows how to do. That same day, he gives the taskmasters a new order: stop giving the people straw to make bricks. Let them gather it themselves, and keep the number of bricks the same. They're lazy, he says; that's why they're crying, let us go. Make the work heavier, so they won't listen to lies. The people scatter all over Egypt looking for stubble. They can't keep up. The Israelite foremen are beaten. And who do they blame? Not Pharaoh. Moses and Aaron. You've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes, they say; you've put a sword in their hand to kill us. Moses turns to God, and he doesn't hold back. Why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? Since I came, it's only gotten worse. The first try failed. The people turned on their leader, and the leader turned to God with a complaint. And God doesn't scold him. God says: now you'll see what I'll do to Pharaoh.
